entries_new.name: William Walker's Nicaragua
entries_new.founder: William Walker, American physician, lawyer and journalist
entries_new.stopped_by: Allied Central American Army (Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua); surrender to US Navy commander Charles Henry Davis
entries_new.pop: 58 men on arrival; a Purdue summary of historian Robert May's work says more than 2,500 filibusters helped him secure the country
entries_new.laws: Slavery legalised; settler land grants of 250 or 350 acres
entries_new.challenge: Costa Rica declared war in March 1856; four neighbouring states and Nicaraguan forces fought him; Cornelius Vanderbilt cut off his shipping
entries_new.recognition: US minister John H. Wheeler recognised the coalition government in 1855; Wikipedia's filibuster article says President Pierce gave recognition in 1856
entries_new.mechanism: Hired by one side in a civil war, he captured the rival capital and ran the government through a puppet president while offering land to American settlers.
entries_new.story:
A civil war in Nicaragua gave the American William Walker his opening. The Democratic Party faction invited him in, and he arrived in June 1855 with 58 men. In October he captured Granada, the rival capital, and installed Patricio Rivas as president while holding real power himself as army chief. His government offered settlers 250 acres, or 350 with a family, and legalised slavery.
Costa Rica declared war in March 1856, and El Salvador and Guatemala sent troops. Walker lost Granada in December 1856 and surrendered to a US Navy commander on 1 May 1857. Two later expeditions ended in arrest, and Honduras executed him in September 1860.

sources.t: Purdue News: Robert May on filibustering

entries_new.name: Republic of Baja California and Sonora
entries_new.founder: William Walker; Henry P. Watkins as vice president
entries_new.stopped_by: Mexican army and local civilians including a group under Antonio María Meléndrez; lack of supplies; mutiny; US military at San Diego
entries_new.pop: 45 men at departure; Wikipedia also gives 200 in one passage
entries_new.laws: Civil code and code of procedure of the state of Louisiana
entries_new.challenge: Mexican government and residents; a US court tried Walker for conducting an illegal war, and the jury acquitted him
entries_new.mechanism: A small armed party seized a thinly settled regional capital, proclaimed a republic, and raised money by selling bonds and land scrip in San Francisco.
entries_new.story:
The American William Walker asked Mexico in 1853 for a grant to set up a colony in Sonora and was refused. He sailed from California with 45 men, captured La Paz, capital of Baja California, and proclaimed a republic on 3 November 1853 (one article gives 200 men; another gives 10 January 1854 for the declaration). He adopted the civil code of Louisiana, a slave state, and later declared a larger Republic of Sonora, though he never controlled Sonora. San Francisco backers bought its bonds.
Short of supplies and facing Mexican forces and desertion, he surrendered to the US military at San Diego in 1854. The jury took eight minutes to acquit him.

entries_new.name: Narciso López's Cuba expeditions
entries_new.founder: Narciso López, Venezuelan-born former Spanish Army general
entries_new.stopped_by: US President Taylor's blockade in 1849; Spanish forces in 1850 and 1851
entries_new.pop: About 600 in 1849 and 1850; several hundred in 1851
entries_new.challenge: The US seized his ships in 1849 and a federal grand jury indicted him and supporters; Spain captured and executed him
entries_new.mechanism: Exile-led volunteers recruited in the US landed in Cuba expecting a local uprising, with backers hoping Cuba would join the Union as a slave state.
entries_new.story:
Narciso López, a former Spanish general, fled Cuba for the United States in 1848 and planned to end Spanish rule there. In 1849 President Zachary Taylor had his ships blockaded and seized, and the 600 volunteers on Round Island, Mississippi, went home. In May 1850 about 600 men reached Cuba and took Cárdenas, but local people sided with Spain, and López retreated to Key West. A federal grand jury indicted him and his backers; there were no convictions, though Governor John Quitman of Mississippi resigned to face trial.
In August 1851 he landed again with several hundred men. Spain captured them and executed most, including López, garroted in Havana on 1 September. His flag later became Cuba's.

entries_new.name: Raousset-Boulbon's Sonora expeditions
entries_new.founder: Count Gaston de Raousset-Boulbon, French adventurer
entries_new.stopped_by: Mexican forces under General Miguel Blanco (1852) and José María Yáñez at Guaymas (1854)
entries_new.challenge: Government of Mexico and Sonora
entries_new.mechanism: Mercenaries entered Sonora under cover of a mining company, aiming to split the state off from Mexico as Texas had split.
entries_new.story: Count Gaston de Raousset-Boulbon, a French aristocrat who had failed as a California gold prospector, sailed mercenaries from San Francisco to Sonora, Mexico, twice. His aim was an independent Sonora on the model of Texas, to be ruled by a French prince. The first trip, in 1852, was presented as a mining company, the Compañía Restauradora de la Mina de la Arizona. His force captured Hermosillo, the state capital, then retreated to Guaymas and surrendered. He returned in 1854 without the popular support he needed and lost the Battle of Guaymas on 13 July. A firing squad executed him there on 13 August 1854.

entries_new.name: Gutiérrez-Magee Expedition
entries_new.founder: Bernardo Gutiérrez de Lara; Augustus William Magee
entries_new.stopped_by: Royalist army of about 1,830 under General Joaquín de Arredondo at the Battle of Medina
entries_new.pop: 130 at the start; roughly 1,400 at Medina
entries_new.laws: Constitution of 18 articles; Roman Catholicism official; private property inviolable
entries_new.challenge: Spanish colonial government of Texas
entries_new.mechanism: A volunteer army crossed from Louisiana, took Spanish towns, and set up a government that declared Texas independent as a part of a wider Mexican republic.
entries_new.story:
In 1812 the Mexican insurgent Bernardo Gutiérrez de Lara and the American officer Augustus Magee crossed from Louisiana into Spanish Texas with 130 men and took Nacogdoches. Governor Salcedo surrendered at San Antonio on 1 April 1813, and prisoners marched out of town were tied to trees and killed. Gutiérrez declared Texas independent on 6 April, and a constitution of 18 articles followed on 17 April.
The Battle of Medina destroyed the army: fewer than 100 republicans escaped, while the royalists lost 55. Mexican histories treat this as part of the independence war; Anglo-American accounts have treated it as a filibuster, an unauthorised private invasion.

entries_new.name: Long Expedition
entries_new.founder: James Long, a doctor from Natchez, Mississippi
entries_new.stopped_by: Spanish troops (500 in 1819; Ignacio Pérez in 1821); US authorities arrested 50 would-be recruits
entries_new.pop: About 200 at the start, 300 at the 1819 peak, 52 in 1821
entries_new.laws: Land grants of 10 square miles to each member; declaration promised religious and press freedom and free trade
entries_new.challenge: Spain; Jean Lafitte, Long's would-be ally, was a Spanish spy
entries_new.mechanism: Volunteers angry at the Adams-Onís Treaty entered Texas, declared a republic, and granted land to members to raise money and followers.
entries_new.story:
When the Adams-Onís Treaty of 1819 fixed the US border at the Sabine River, men in Natchez, Mississippi, gathered to take Texas anyway and elected James Long, a doctor, as leader. He had pledges of over $500,000. At Nacogdoches on 22 June 1819 they formed a government with a 21-member council, declared independence, and allotted 10 square miles to each member. Five hundred Spanish troops drove them out that autumn.
Long returned in 1820. On 4 October 1821 he took Presidio La Bahía with 52 men and surrendered four days later. He was sent to Mexico City, where a guard killed him.

entries_new.name: Republic of Fredonia
entries_new.founder: Haden Edwards, a land agent (empresario) holding a Mexican colonisation contract
entries_new.stopped_by: Over 100 Mexican soldiers and 275 Texian militia
entries_new.pop: Edwards's settlers and supporters
entries_new.challenge: Mexico revoked Edwards's contract; the Cherokee first signed a treaty and then repudiated it; Stephen F. Austin opposed the revolt
entries_new.mechanism: Settlers arrested local officials and declared independence over the land Mexico had granted their leader, with a treaty offered to the Cherokee.
entries_new.story:
Haden Edwards received a Mexican land grant around Nacogdoches, Texas, in 1825. Disputes with families already there led Mexico to revoke his contract. In December 1826 his supporters arrested municipal officials and declared the Republic of Fredonia. The Cherokee signed a treaty of support, then repudiated it after approaches from Mexican officials and the settler leader Stephen F. Austin, and Chief Fields was killed by his own tribe.
On 31 January 1827 over 100 Mexican soldiers and 275 Texian militia entered Nacogdoches, and the Edwards brothers fled to the United States. Mexico then sharply curtailed immigration from the US. Some historians treat the revolt as the start of the Texas Revolution.

entries_new.name: Republic of the Floridas on Amelia Island
entries_new.founder: Gregor MacGregor, Scottish adventurer; then Louis-Michel Aury
entries_new.stopped_by: US naval force, 23 December 1817
entries_new.challenge: Spain held the island; the United States captured it, and President Monroe called the venture a mere private, unauthorized adventure
entries_new.mechanism: A small force seized a Spanish island used by smugglers, formed a council and constitution, and invited all Florida to join against Spain.
entries_new.story:
Amelia Island, off Spanish Florida, was a smugglers' resort with sometimes 150 ships in harbour. In June 1817 the Scottish adventurer Gregor MacGregor, claiming a commission from Simón Bolívar, overran it with a small force after most recruits for a larger invasion deserted. He left for Nassau in September.
Louis-Michel Aury, previously a buccaneer leader at Galveston, then took control, set up a Supreme Council of the Floridas with a constitution, and flew the flag of revolutionary Mexico. A US naval force captured the island on 23 December 1817. President Monroe told Congress it was a channel for slaves illegally imported from Africa and for smuggling.

entries_new.name: State of Muskogee
entries_new.founder: William Augustus Bowles, a Loyalist veteran living among the Muscogee
entries_new.stopped_by: Spain and the United States; Benjamin Hawkins trapped him at a council at Tuckabatchee
entries_new.pop: Backed by Miccosukee (Seminole) and several Muscogee bands; a few English adventurers ran the administration
entries_new.challenge: Spain sent forces against it and besieged it; the US Indian agent Benjamin Hawkins laid the trap that ended it
entries_new.mechanism: A Loyalist adventurer with Native allies proclaimed a state in Spanish Florida, declared the 1796 US-Spain treaty void, and ran a small navy against Spanish ships.
entries_new.story:
William Augustus Bowles, a Maryland Loyalist who married into Muscogee families, landed at Apalachicola Bay in 1799 and named himself Director General of the Muskogee Nation. On 31 October he declared Pinckney's Treaty between Spain and the US void because it ignored Native sovereignty over Florida. He welcomed runaway slaves, kept a three-ship navy, and moved his capital to Miccosukee under Spanish attack.
His siege of San Marcos failed in 1802. After the Treaty of Amiens brought peace in Europe, the Seminoles signed with Spain. In 1803 Hawkins, the US Indian agent, had him seized at a council and delivered to the Spanish governor in Pensacola.

entries_new.name: Ungern-Sternberg in Mongolia
entries_new.founder: Baron Roman von Ungern-Sternberg, a Russian officer turned independent warlord
entries_new.stopped_by: Red Army with Mongolian rebels; he was captured, tried and executed
entries_new.challenge: China's garrison, which he expelled; then the Red Army and Mongolian rebels
entries_new.mechanism: A warlord's cavalry division drove out a foreign garrison, restored a local monarch, and ruled the capital by force behind him.
entries_new.story:
Baron Roman von Ungern-Sternberg, a Baltic German monarchist in the Russian Civil War, formed the volunteer Asiatic Cavalry Division. China had sent troops into Outer Mongolia in 1919 despite a 1915 agreement securing its autonomy. On 4 February 1921 Ungern took the capital, now Ulaanbaatar, and restored the Bogd Khan to power.
His five-month occupation relied on what Wikipedia describes as fear and brutal violence against Bolsheviks and Chinese. In June he went into Siberia to pre-empt a joint Red Army and Mongolian rebel invasion and was captured two months later. After a six-hour show trial at Novonikolayevsk he was executed on 15 September 1921.

entries_new.name: Crabb Expedition
entries_new.founder: Henry A. Crabb, former California state senator
entries_new.stopped_by: Mexican liberal forces under Ignacio Pesqueira with O'odham allies
entries_new.pop: About 100 recruited, against 1,000 authorised; 85 at Caborca by one count
entries_new.challenge: Mexico; the local leader who invited him turned on him
entries_new.mechanism: Invited to bring colonists to help one side in a Mexican civil conflict, the party arrived after that side had already won.
entries_new.story:
Henry Crabb, a Tennessee judge's son and former California state senator, accepted an offer from the Sonoran rebel Ignacio Pesqueira to bring 1,000 colonists to northern Mexico. He left San Diego in January 1857 with about 100 men on a private venture not directed by the US government. By the time he arrived, Pesqueira had won and his followers objected to American aid.
At Caborca in April 1857 the party held an adobe building for eight days until an O'odham warrior set it alight. After they surrendered, they were shot by firing squad. Accounts differ on the numbers: about 50 of 85 survivors in one, 58 executed in a letter by George Cardwell.

entries_new.name: Blount Conspiracy
entries_new.founder: William Blount, US senator from Tennessee; John Chisholm, Indian agent
entries_new.stopped_by: Exposure of Blount's letter; expulsion from the Senate
entries_new.challenge: US Senate expelled him; he was the first federal official to face impeachment
entries_new.mechanism: Territorial militias, with Royal Navy help, were to seize Spanish Louisiana and Florida for Britain, raising the value of the plotter's frontier land.
entries_new.story: William Blount, a US senator and heavy land speculator in debt, feared France would gain Spanish Louisiana and close the Mississippi River. With the Indian agent John Chisholm he planned for American territorial militias, aided by the Royal Navy, to attack New Madrid, New Orleans and Pensacola and hand the region to Britain. In April 1797 the merchant James Carey gave a government agent a letter from Blount describing the plan, and it reached President Adams. The Senate expelled Blount in 1797, and he became the first federal official to face impeachment. He stayed popular in Tennessee and served in its state senate.
entries_new.anchor: Knoxville, Tennessee (plotter's base; the target was Spanish Louisiana and Florida)

entries_new.name: Republic of East Florida
entries_new.founder: General George Mathews, commissioned by President Madison
entries_new.stopped_by: Withdrawal of US units; Seminole entry into the conflict
entries_new.pop: About 125 Patriots in March 1812
entries_new.challenge: Spain; British ambassador Augustus Foster protested
entries_new.mechanism: Georgia volunteers calling themselves Patriots took a Spanish town and immediately offered it to the United States, with US gunboats and troops in support.
entries_new.story:
The Patriot War was a 1812 attempt to start a rebellion in Spanish East Florida so that the US could annex it. It shows how blurred filibustering could be: General George Mathews held a commission from President Madison, and US gunboats, soldiers and marines helped, though the Patriot Army was mainly Georgia citizens.
On 17 March 1812 about 125 Patriots entered Fernandina, raised their flag, and offered the town to US Colonel Smith, who accepted. The occupation lasted over a year but never had the strength to attack St. Augustine. The Patriots dissolved after US units withdrew and the Seminoles entered the conflict.

entries_new.name: Republic of West Florida
entries_new.founder: Philemon Thomas (armed rebels); Fulwar Skipwith, elected governor
entries_new.stopped_by: United States occupation under President Madison's proclamation of 27 October 1810
entries_new.pop: Baton Rouge District population almost entirely Anglo-American
entries_new.challenge: Spain lost the fort; the US declared the area already part of the Louisiana Purchase and occupied it
entries_new.recognition: None; Spain and the US disputed the land
entries_new.mechanism: Armed settlers stormed a Spanish fort, elected a government, and asked the US to annex them, then objected when annexation came without their terms.
entries_new.story:
Americans had moved in numbers into Spanish West Florida, and some were land speculators. On 23 September 1810 armed rebels under Philemon Thomas stormed Fort San Carlos at Baton Rouge, killed two Spanish soldiers, and captured the district governor. They raised a blue flag with a white star, chose St. Francisville as capital, and on 7 November elected Fulwar Skipwith, a former US diplomat, as governor.
The republic asked the US for annexation and money. Madison proclaimed the area already part of the Louisiana Purchase and sent officials to occupy it. Skipwith protested that the people would not submit without conditions. The US occupied it in December 1810, after just over 2.5 months.

entries_new.name: Miranda's 1806 Venezuela expedition
entries_new.founder: Francisco de Miranda, Venezuelan revolutionary; William S. Smith
entries_new.stopped_by: Spanish forces at Ocumare and Coro
entries_new.pop: 200 volunteers at the start; about 220 at Coro
entries_new.challenge: Spain; the US indicted Smith and the shipowner Ogden; Caracas condemned Miranda to death in his absence
entries_new.mechanism: A privately raised force from New York, and then British naval support from Trinidad, tried to land in Spanish Venezuela and start a revolt.
entries_new.story:
Francisco de Miranda raised funds and about 200 volunteers in New York and sailed for Venezuela on 2 February 1806 on the hired ship Leander. Jefferson and Madison met him without involving the US. On 28 April a landing at Ocumare failed: 60 men were tried for piracy, and 10 were sentenced to death.
With British naval support from Trinidad, he landed at La Vela de Coro in August and took Santa Ana de Coro, but residents gave no support. He left on 13 August as Spanish forces arrived. A New York grand jury indicted Smith and Ogden for piracy and violating the Neutrality Act of 1794.

entries_new.name: Quitman's planned invasion of Cuba
entries_new.founder: John A. Quitman, former governor of Mississippi
entries_new.stopped_by: The Pierce administration, which reversed course in May 1854
entries_new.pop: Several thousand men said to be ready
entries_new.challenge: The US government stopped it
entries_new.mechanism: With early encouragement from the President, a former governor organised a private invasion force to bring Cuba in as slave territory.
entries_new.story: John Quitman resigned as governor of Mississippi in 1851 after arrest over his aid to Narciso López's Cuba expedition; the charges were dropped after three hung juries. With encouragement from President Pierce he began preparing his own invasion of Cuba in July 1853, and several thousand men were ready when the administration reversed course in May 1854 and moved to stop it. Wikipedia suggests the reason was fear that adding slave territory after the Kansas-Nebraska Act would damage the Democratic Party in the North. Elected to Congress in 1855, Quitman introduced a bill to repeal most of the Neutrality Act of 1818.
entries_new.anchor: Natchez, Mississippi (organiser's home; the target was Cuba)

entries_new.name: Ira Allen's United Columbia
entries_new.founder: Ira Allen, a founder of Vermont
entries_new.stopped_by: Capture at sea; British trial
entries_new.pop: None
entries_new.challenge: Britain tried him on a charge of furnishing arms for Irish rebels; he was acquitted after an eight-year lawsuit
entries_new.mechanism: A frontier leader bought French arms to seize Canada and create an independent republic.
entries_new.story: Ira Allen, a founder of Vermont and younger brother of Ethan Allen, went to France in 1795 seeking French help to seize Canada and create an independent republic called United Columbia. He bought 20,000 muskets and 24 cannons but was captured at sea and taken to England. There he was tried on a charge of furnishing arms for Irish rebels. The lawsuit lasted eight years and ended in acquittal, with an Admiralty judge summoned before the Court of King's Bench for the first time.
entries_new.anchor: Burlington, Vermont (founder's base; the target was Canada)

entries_new.name: Fenian raids on Canada
entries_new.founder: Fenian Brotherhood, an Irish republican group based in the US
entries_new.stopped_by: Canadian militia and British forces; US Navy gunboat Michigan; US arrests
entries_new.pop: Over 700 at Campobello; 600 to 700 at Ridgeway; 1,000 to 1,500 at Pigeon Hill; about 35 in Manitoba in 1871
entries_new.challenge: Britain and Canada; US authorities arrested men and confiscated arms, though some speculated that parts of the US government ignored the preparations
entries_new.mechanism: Civil War veterans crossed from the US to seize Canadian targets as a way of pressing Britain to leave Ireland.
entries_new.story:
The Fenian Brotherhood, Irish republicans based in the US, sent incursions into British North America in 1866 and from 1870 to 1871 to pressure Britain to withdraw from Ireland. Over 700 gathered against Campobello Island in April 1866 and dispersed before British warships. In June they beat Canadian militia at Ridgeway, then surrendered to the US Navy on the way home. Another 1,000 to 1,500 held Pigeon Hill. A 1870 raid was turned back at Eccles Hill.
In October 1871 about 35 men took a Hudson's Bay post in Manitoba that a survey placed inside the US. Wikipedia lists the raids as one factor in Canadian Confederation.

entries_new.name: Genêt's planned attack on Spanish Louisiana and Florida
entries_new.founder: Edmond-Charles Genêt, French envoy; volunteers including George Rogers Clark, listed by Wikipedia among filibusters
entries_new.stopped_by: President Washington's government, which asked France to recall Genêt
entries_new.challenge: President Washington declared neutrality on 22 April 1793; Jefferson told Genêt his actions were unacceptable
entries_new.mechanism: A foreign envoy raised American volunteers and privateers on US soil to attack Spanish lands, which helped prompt the first US neutrality law.
entries_new.story: Edmond-Charles Genêt arrived in Charleston as French envoy in April 1793 and commissioned four privateers. Working with the French consul, he organised American volunteers to fight Britain's Spanish allies in Florida, and a militia prepared to move against the Spanish. President Washington had declared US neutrality on 22 April; Secretary of State Jefferson told Genêt his actions were unacceptable, and Washington asked France to recall him. The new government in France issued a warrant for Genêt's arrest, and he stayed in the US on asylum. Wikipedia's list of filibusters includes George Rogers Clark for this period.
entries_new.anchor: Charleston, South Carolina (organiser's base; the target was Spanish Florida and Louisiana)

entries_new.name: Carbajal's Republic of Sierra Madre
entries_new.founder: José María Jesús Carbajal, Mexican-Tejano surveyor and politician
entries_new.stopped_by: Mexican General Francisco Avalos; National Guard from Ciudad Victoria; US arrests
entries_new.pop: Included thirty Texas Rangers under John S. Ford
entries_new.challenge: Mexico; a grand jury in Brownsville indicted him under the Neutrality Act of 1818, and the charges were dismissed in 1854
entries_new.cost: Seed money from selling Mexican land grants to Texas merchants; a $6,000 family loan
entries_new.mechanism: Troops from Texas took Mexican border towns and cut customs duties there, financed by Texas merchants who wanted lower tariffs.
entries_new.story:
In 1851 José María Jesús Carbajal sought a federalist state in northern Mexico, the Republic of Sierra Madre. The fight, known as the Merchants War, grew from high Mexican tariffs and from bounty hunting of slaves who had fled Texas. He raised money by selling land grants to Texas merchants. On 19 September his force took Camargo and cut its tariffs, and on 6 October it took Reynosa. A ten-day attack on Matamoros failed, and he retreated from Cerralvo in November.
A Brownsville grand jury indicted him under the Neutrality Act of 1818 in January 1852. A later case ended in 1855 without prosecution.

entries_new.name: Burr conspiracy
entries_new.founder: Aaron Burr, former US vice president; Harman Blennerhassett; General James Wilkinson
entries_new.stopped_by: General Wilkinson's letter to Jefferson; arrest on Jefferson's orders
entries_new.pop: Accounts range from fewer than 40 men to upwards of 7,000
entries_new.challenge: The US charged him with treason; Chief Justice Marshall's ruling led to acquittal because no overt act of war was proved
entries_new.mechanism: A former vice president gathered men and supplies on a private island on the Ohio River; his aims are still disputed.
entries_new.story:
Aaron Burr, US vice president until 1805, was accused of planning to form an independent country from the western US, or to invade Spanish territory. Burr's own account was that he planned to farm 40,000 acres in Spanish Texas. Historians still disagree, and estimates of his followers run from under 40 to over 7,000.
He stored men and supplies on Blennerhassett Island in the Ohio River. His key partner, General James Wilkinson, sent Jefferson a letter claiming to show treason. Burr surrendered at Bayou Pierre, escaped, and was recaptured on 19 February 1807. Marshall ruled that treason needed an overt act of war, and Burr was acquitted.

entries_new.name: Thomas Jordan's landing in Cuba
entries_new.founder: Thomas Jordan, former Confederate general
entries_new.stopped_by: Shortage of supplies; he resigned
entries_new.pop: 300 men, with arms for 6,000 more
entries_new.challenge: Spain, in the Ten Years' War
entries_new.mechanism: A former Confederate general landed men and arms from abroad to join the Cuban insurgency against Spain.
entries_new.story: Thomas Jordan, a former Confederate general, became chief of staff of the Cuban insurgent army in the Ten Years' War against Spain. Wikipedia lists him among American filibusters, meaning private military adventurers acting without their government's approval. In May 1869 he landed at Mayarí with 300 men and enough arms and ammunition for the 6,000 more he hoped would join. He became military head of the insurgent army in December and won at Guaimaro in January 1870. Extremely short of supplies, he resigned a month later and returned to the US.

entries_new.name: Samuel Brannan's Hawaii venture
entries_new.founder: Samuel Brannan, California businessman and first newspaper publisher in San Francisco
entries_new.mechanism: A wealthy Californian led what press reports called a filibuster to Hawaii and bought land in Honolulu.
entries_new.story: Samuel Brannan, a California businessman and early Mormon leader, is listed by Wikipedia among American filibusters for Hawaii, then a kingdom. Newspapers of the time described his mission as little more than a colonising scheme, and the Daily Evening Picayune later softened its wording to an emigrating company. His biography records that he visited Hawaii in 1851 and purchased large amounts of land in Honolulu. The sources read for this entry give no account of any armed action there.

entries_new.name: Kinney's Mosquito Coast colony
entries_new.founder: Henry L. Kinney, Texas politician and founder of Corpus Christi; Joseph W. Fabens
entries_new.stopped_by: US Navy blockade in New York; Nicaragua; William Walker
entries_new.pop: 100 men or more in August 1855, by his own letter
entries_new.laws: His followers gave him authority to raise armies and declare martial law
entries_new.challenge: US and Nicaraguan governments; shipping tycoon Cornelius Vanderbilt; Walker annexed his land
entries_new.cost: Largely financed by New York backers
entries_new.mechanism: A Texas politician bought land claims in Nicaragua on dubious legal grounds, sailed with armed followers, and had them elect him governor.
entries_new.story:
Henry Kinney, founder of what became Corpus Christi, bought millions of acres in Nicaragua in 1854 under what Wikipedia calls dubious legal circumstances, with New York backers, intending a colony on the coast then dominated by Britain. In February 1855 he was warned this might break the Neutrality Act of 1794. He was arrested in New York in April and his ship blockaded by the US Navy.
Released on bail, he reached Central America with about 100 men by August. His followers elected him governor; he flew a flag and started a newspaper. A revolt failed, and in February 1856 William Walker annexed his land.

entries_new.name: Thirty-Three Orientals
entries_new.founder: Juan Antonio Lavalleja and Manuel Oribe
entries_new.stopped_by: No one finally stopped it: mediation by Britain's Viscount Ponsonby produced an independent state in 1828
entries_new.pop: 33 by name; the true number is disputed
entries_new.challenge: Empire of Brazil, which had annexed the province in 1824 and declared war in December 1825
entries_new.recognition: United Provinces of the Río de la Plata in 1825; independence settled by the Preliminary Peace Convention of 1828
entries_new.cost: Backed by Buenos Aires ranchers and beef-curers, with Juan Manuel de Rosas a key financier
entries_new.mechanism: A small party landed by boat, raised the countryside, formed an assembly, and pulled a neighbouring state and then a mediator into the dispute.
entries_new.story:
Brazil annexed the Oriental Province, today's Uruguay, in February 1824. Lavalleja organised an expedition from Buenos Aires, paid for in part by ranchers and meat-curers who saw Brazilian rule as a threat to their business. The group crossed the Uruguay River and landed at Agraciada Beach at dawn on 19 April 1825. It raised rural support, and on 25 August an assembly declared independence from Brazil and allegiance to the United Provinces.
Brazil declared war in December. After British mediation, the Preliminary Peace Convention of August 1828 set up a state independent of both. It is one of the few private landings here that ended in a lasting state, though only with neighbouring states in the war.

entries_new.name: Expedition of the Thousand
entries_new.founder: Giuseppe Garibaldi
entries_new.stopped_by: No one militarily: a plebiscite joined the conquests to Piedmont-Sardinia
entries_new.pop: Around 1,000 at the start; later the larger Southern Army
entries_new.challenge: Kingdom of the Two Sicilies
entries_new.recognition: Its conquest was joined to Piedmont-Sardinia by plebiscite
entries_new.mechanism: A volunteer corps conquered a whole kingdom and handed it to another monarchy rather than ruling it as its own state.
entries_new.story: In 1860 about 1,000 volunteers under Giuseppe Garibaldi sailed from near Genoa and landed at Marsala, Sicily, to conquer the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, which had a larger army and navy. Reinforced by southern volunteers, they took the entire kingdom within a few months. Garibaldi acted in the name of King Victor Emmanuel II. A plebiscite then brought Naples and Sicily into Piedmont-Sardinia, and the Kingdom of Italy followed on 17 March 1861. Historians including Dominic Alessio have proposed Garibaldi as a filibuster outside the Americas, and some American newspapers of the time used the word; Wikipedia warns that this use may be anachronistic.

entries_new.name: Virginius Affair
entries_new.founder: Cuban insurgents; John F. Patterson as secret buyer; Captain Joseph Fry
entries_new.stopped_by: Spanish warship Tornado, 30 October 1873
entries_new.pop: 53 executed
entries_new.challenge: Spain tried those aboard as pirates; Britain intervened to stop the executions
entries_new.mechanism: A former blockade runner was secretly bought for Cuban insurgents to land men and arms during the Ten Years' War.
entries_new.story: The Virginius was a fast former Confederate blockade runner bought in 1870 by John Patterson, acting secretly for the Cuban insurgent Manuel de Quesada, to land men and arms in Cuba. On 30 October 1873 the Spanish warship Tornado chased and captured it six miles off Cuba. Spain tried everyone on board as pirates. It shot four insurgent leaders on 4 November and executed 53 men in all at Santiago de Cuba, many American and British, before British intervention stopped the killing. War talk faded by the end of December, and Spain paid compensation to British and then other families, with the matter closed in February 1875.

entries_new.name: Louis-Michel Aury at Galveston and Old Providence
entries_new.founder: Louis-Michel Aury, French privateer
entries_new.stopped_by: Aury's death on 30 August 1821
entries_new.pop: 400 men and 14 ships at Old Providence
entries_new.challenge: Spain; attacks on Trujillo and Omoa were repulsed in 1820; he quarrelled with Bolívar
entries_new.mechanism: A privateer used commissions from new republics to hold islands as bases, living off captured Spanish cargo.
entries_new.story:
Louis-Michel Aury was a French privateer, a private ship captain licensed by a government to seize enemy vessels. In September 1816 he set up a base on Galveston Island as commissioner for the fledgling Mexican republic and smuggled enslaved people from it. In 1817 he carried Francisco Mina's force to Soto La Marina and then took over Amelia Island until US forces arrived.
On 4 July 1818 he captured Old Providence Island in the Caribbean with 400 men and 14 ships, building a settlement around captured Spanish cargo and a fort on neighbouring Saint Catherine. His 1820 attacks on Trujillo and Omoa failed. He died in 1821.

entries_new.name: Champ d'Asile
entries_new.founder: General Charles Lallemand, a Bonapartist veteran
entries_new.stopped_by: Spanish governor Antonio María Martínez sent troops; the site was abandoned
entries_new.pop: 20 founders in January 1818; 120 volunteers came in March
entries_new.challenge: Spanish authorities in Texas
entries_new.mechanism: French veterans built forts in disputed Texas under the name of a farm colony.
entries_new.story: Champ d'Asile, meaning Field of Asylum, was a settlement on the Trinity River in Texas founded in 1818 by French veterans loyal to Napoleon under General Charles Lallemand. It was presented as a colony for grapes and olives, but there was little sign of farming on the site, while a fortress and munitions works were begun. Lallemand financed it through land speculation. Reports of it worried settlers in New Spain, and the governor, Antonio María Martínez, sent troops toward San Marcos. The settlers abandoned the site in July 1818, as the US and Spain were negotiating their border.

entries_new.name: Hippolyte Bouchard's capture of Monterey
entries_new.founder: Hippolyte Bouchard, French-born Argentine corsair
entries_new.stopped_by: He left after six days
entries_new.challenge: Spain
entries_new.mechanism: A privateer under an Argentine commission seized a Spanish colonial capital and raised a foreign flag, then sailed on.
entries_new.story: Hippolyte Bouchard was a French-born sailor who became an Argentine corsair, a privately armed raider licensed by a government. On a long voyage against Spanish colonies he blockaded Manila and recovered an Argentine privateer in Hawaii. His forces then occupied Monterey in Spanish California, raised the Argentine flag, and held the town for six days. He next plundered Mission San Juan Capistrano and raided Spanish ports in Central America. Wikipedia's filibuster article lists him among non-American filibusters, though he sailed under a commission and held no territory for long.

entries_new.name: Jameson Raid
entries_new.founder: Leander Starr Jameson, employed by Cecil Rhodes
entries_new.stopped_by: Transvaal forces at Doornkop
entries_new.pop: 500 British South Africa Company police
entries_new.challenge: South African Republic; the British Colonial Secretary ordered it repudiated
entries_new.mechanism: Company police rode into a neighbouring republic expecting expatriate workers to rise; the rising never came.
entries_new.story:
From 29 December 1895 Leander Starr Jameson led 500 British South Africa Company police from Rhodesia into the Transvaal, working for Cecil Rhodes. The plan relied on a revolt by foreign workers in Johannesburg, which did not happen. Boer forces tracked the column from the border because the telegraph to Pretoria was left intact. Jameson surrendered at Doornkop on 2 January 1896 after losing about thirty men.
The Boers handed the raiders to Britain for trial. Reform Committee members in Johannesburg were found guilty of high treason and sentenced to death, later commuted, and released on fines by June 1896. Rhodes was replaced as prime minister of the Cape Colony.

entries_new.name: Magonista rebellion in Baja California
entries_new.founder: Liberal Party of Mexico; Ricardo Flores Magón, planning from Los Angeles
entries_new.stopped_by: Federal forces under Colonel Celso Vega; forces loyal to Madero; arrests in the US
entries_new.pop: About 400 reported in the Mexicali Valley in April
entries_new.challenge: Mexico under Díaz, then Madero; leaders were arrested in the US on a tip from Madero's agents
entries_new.mechanism: An exiled party in Los Angeles sent mixed American and Mexican fighters to hold border towns as a base for a social revolution.
entries_new.story: The Liberal Party of Mexico, run from Los Angeles, tried to create a liberated territory in Baja California as a base for social revolution. Its fighters took Mexicali on 29 January 1911 and also held Tijuana, controlling them for about six months. A force of 126 under John R. Mosby occupied Tecate in April. Some of the rebels sought to abolish property and set up an anarchist commune. Wikipedia quotes a judgment that dissensions among Americans, Mexicans and Indians crippled them. Lacking volunteers and ammunition, they were pushed back, and federal troops retook Tijuana. Leaders were arrested in the US.

entries_new.name: Zemurray and Lee Christmas's Honduras invasion
entries_new.founder: Samuel Zemurray, banana magnate of Cuyamel Fruit; Lee Christmas, American mercenary; Manuel Bonilla
entries_new.stopped_by: No one: Bonilla took the presidency
entries_new.pop: About 100 mercenaries, plus locals
entries_new.challenge: Honduran government of Miguel Dávila; the action ran against the wishes of the US government
entries_new.mechanism: A company owner hired a mercenary to restore a friendly president because the sitting government's finance deals would raise his costs.
entries_new.story: In 1910 Samuel Zemurray, a banana company owner, wanted a new government in Honduras because President Dávila's planned financial deals would raise his costs. He hired the American mercenary Lee Christmas, a former railway engineer who had changed sides several times, to put Manuel Bonilla back in power, against the wishes of the US government. Christmas hired about 100 mercenaries and carried machine guns on a former US Navy ship. They took Trujillo and Iriona and won the Battle of La Ceiba on 25 January 1911. Bonilla became president again until his death in 1913, with Christmas as military commander.

entries_new.name: Landing of the Granma
entries_new.founder: Fidel Castro and the 26th of July Movement
entries_new.stopped_by: Batista's forces ambushed the landing party at Alegría de Pío; the survivors reached the Sierra Maestra
entries_new.pop: 82 fighters
entries_new.challenge: Government of Fulgencio Batista in Cuba
entries_new.mechanism: Exiles trained abroad sailed a yacht to Cuba to start an armed revolt timed with a rising in Santiago, then fought on as guerrillas after the landing went wrong.
entries_new.story: Castro and 81 others left Tuxpan, Mexico, on the yacht Granma shortly after midnight on 25 November 1956, aiming to overthrow Fulgencio Batista. Wikipedia's filibuster article names Castro among Cuban filibusters. The rising planned in Santiago went ahead on 30 November, but the boat reached Playa las Coloradas only on 2 December, stuck on a sandbar in a mangrove swamp, and the reception party had already left. Aircraft attacked them, and an ambush at Alegría de Pío caused many casualties. Survivors went to the Sierra Maestra mountains to wage guerrilla war.

entries_new.name: Knights of the Golden Circle
entries_new.founder: George W. L. Bickley
entries_new.stopped_by: Civil War drew off its support
entries_new.challenge: Mexico and Central America had no interest in joining; the Civil War ended its schemes
entries_new.mechanism: A secret society planned private conquests around the Caribbean to add slave states.
entries_new.story: The Knights of the Golden Circle was a secret society founded in the US in 1854 by George Bickley. It first aimed to expand the US into Latin America, adding slave states, and later for the southern states to secede and then annex that land. The golden circle had a radius of 16 degrees centred on Havana and covered the Southern US, Mexico, Central America, Cuba and the Caribbean, which Bickley said would produce 25 new slave states. When the Civil War began, the South needed its resources at home, and support for filibustering fell away. Bickley gave up its leadership in early 1863.
entries_new.anchor: Cincinnati, Ohio (where the first branch was set up; the target was the Caribbean rim)

entries_new.name: Benyovszky in Madagascar
entries_new.founder: Count Maurice Benyovszky, Hungarian-born officer and adventurer
entries_new.stopped_by: Sakalava resistance; a small armed force sent by the French governor of Mauritius, which killed him in May 1786
entries_new.challenge: Sakalava people; France, first his sponsor and later his opponent
entries_new.cost: Second voyage backed by Baltimore traders in return for a regular supply of slaves
entries_new.mechanism: An adventurer turned a French-backed trading post into a personal venture, and returned on private American money.
entries_new.story:
Count Maurice Benyovszky escaped Russian exile in Kamchatka and in 1773 agreed with the French government to set up a trading post on Madagascar. It was established at Antongil by March 1774, and he gave it up in 1776 after trouble with the climate, terrain and the Sakalava people. His Memoirs of 1790 are largely fictitious, Wikipedia says.
In 1784 he signed with two Baltimore traders, who invested in return for a regular supply of slaves. His ship reached Madagascar in June 1785 and met Sakalava hostility. The French governor of Mauritius sent a small armed force to close his operation, and he was killed in May 1786.

entries_new.name: New Moscow at Sagallo
entries_new.founder: Nikolay Ashinov, Cossack adventurer
entries_new.stopped_by: French squadron of one cruiser and three gunboats
entries_new.pop: About 150, including women, children and about 40 clergy
entries_new.challenge: France, whose protectorate included the Gulf of Tadjoura
entries_new.mechanism: A religious mission to Ethiopia landed and instead occupied an old fort, declaring the surrounding coast Russian soil.
entries_new.story:
Nikolay Ashinov, a Cossack adventurer, sailed in December 1888 with about 150 people, presented as a religious mission to Ethiopia. They entered the Gulf of Tadjoura, in today's Djibouti and then a French protectorate, on 6 January 1889. He occupied the abandoned Egyptian fort of Sagallo, called it New Moscow, and declared fifty miles of coast and a hundred miles inland to be Russian land.
On 5 February a French squadron gave an ultimatum and then shelled the fort, killing one Cossack and five civilians. Ashinov's group surrendered and was shipped back to Russia, where Tsar Alexander III ordered an investigation.

entries_new.name: George Thomas's kingdom of Hansi
entries_new.founder: George Thomas, Irish mercenary
entries_new.stopped_by: Sikh forces and Patiala's army under Sahib Singh
entries_new.pop: Five to six thousand selected residents at Hansi; army of 6,000 infantry, 1,000 cavalry and 50 cannon
entries_new.challenge: Marathas, whom he left; Phulkian Sikh chiefs
entries_new.mechanism: A deserter turned mercenary used his late patron's death to seize districts, then minted coin and built an arms industry to stay independent.
entries_new.story:
George Thomas, a tenant farmer's son from County Tipperary, deserted the Royal Navy at Madras in 1782 and became a general under Indian rulers. When his Maratha patron died in 1797, he declared independence, took Rohtak and Hisar, and made Hansi his capital, in today's Haryana. He styled himself Raja of Hansi, minted his own rupees, cast artillery and made muskets, and said he resettled five to six thousand people.
Wars with Sikh chiefs followed. In 1801 he was driven out, defeated at Hansi by Patiala's army, and stripped of guns, throne and crown. He retired into British territory and died in 1802.

entries_new.name: Catalan Company in the Duchy of Athens
entries_new.founder: Great Catalan Company, a mercenary band founded under Roger de Flor
entries_new.stopped_by: Navarrese Company and Florentine troops of Nerio I Acciaioli, 1388 to 1390
entries_new.pop: About 8,000 at the start by one chronicle; a Byzantine historian says 1,000
entries_new.challenge: Duke Walter V of Brienne, killed at Halmyros; the Pope and rival claimants objected
entries_new.recognition: Accepted the overlordship of the Aragonese crown of Sicily in 1312
entries_new.mechanism: Unpaid mercenaries beat their employer in battle, took his duchy, and then secured themselves by accepting a distant king as overlord.
entries_new.story:
The Catalan Company was a band of veterans left without work by the 1302 peace in Sicily. It served the Byzantine emperor, then in 1310 the Duke of Athens, Walter V of Brienne. He did not pay the agreed sum, so it fought him at the Battle of Halmyros on 15 March 1311 and won. The Company took his duchy, extended its control to Thebes and Thessaly, and ruled as feudal lords.
In 1312 it accepted the overlordship of the Aragonese crown of Sicily, and it held the duchies as vassals until defeat by the Navarrese Company in 1388 to 1390.

entries_new.name: Francesco Sforza takes Milan
entries_new.founder: Francesco I Sforza, an Italian mercenary captain (condottiere)
entries_new.stopped_by: Not stopped by force in his lifetime
entries_new.challenge: Ambrosian Republic; formal title lagged for decades
entries_new.recognition: City senate handed him the duchy; formal investiture by the Emperor came only for his son Ludovico in 1494
entries_new.mechanism: A hired general married the ruling family, blockaded the city that had declared a republic, and accepted its surrender as duke.
entries_new.story: Francesco Sforza was an Italian condottiere, a commander who sold his army's services by contract. He served the Papal States and Milan, and married Bianca Maria Visconti, daughter of the Duke of Milan. When the duke died without a male heir in 1447, Milan declared the Ambrosian Republic. Sforza gained other cities and planned its conquest. In 1450, after years of famine and riots, the senate entrusted the duchy to him, and he entered as duke on 26 February. Wikipedia calls him one of the few condottieri to turn battle success into stable dynastic rule. Formal imperial investiture came only in 1494, for his son.

entries_new.name: Rainulf Drengot's county of Aversa
entries_new.founder: Rainulf Drengot, Norman adventurer and mercenary
entries_new.stopped_by: Not stopped in his lifetime; he died in 1045
entries_new.pop: A band of 250 at the start
entries_new.challenge: Byzantine Empire; rival Lombard lords
entries_new.recognition: Duke Sergius IV of Naples gave him Aversa; Emperor Conrad II recognised his title in 1037
entries_new.mechanism: Exiled warriors sold their services to whichever local lord paid most until one paid in land and a title.
entries_new.story: Rainulf Drengot was exiled from Normandy and came to southern Italy with brothers and 250 fighters around 1017. Amatus of Montecassino, a chronicler, says they sold their services to whoever offered most and never let any Lombard lord win outright. In 1030 Duke Sergius IV of Naples gave Rainulf the stronghold of Aversa, the title of count, and his sister in marriage. Emperor Conrad II recognised the title in 1037. After beating the Byzantines in 1038, Rainulf declared himself prince and independent of Naples, and took a neighbouring principality. This was the start of Norman rule in southern Italy, according to the sequence given by the article.

entries_new.name: El Cid's Principality of Valencia
entries_new.founder: Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar (El Cid), an exiled Castilian knight
entries_new.stopped_by: Moors retook Valencia in 1102
entries_new.challenge: Muslim rulers of the region
entries_new.mechanism: An exiled knight who fought for both Christian and Muslim rulers took a city with his own followers and ruled it himself.
entries_new.story: Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, known as El Cid, was a Castilian knight exiled by King Alfonso VI in 1081. He found work with Muslim as well as Christian rulers and, at the head of his own knights, came to dominate the eastern Iberian coast. He ruled the Principality of Valencia from 17 June 1094 until his death in 1099. His wife, Jimena Díaz, inherited the city and held it until the Moors retook it in 1102.

entries_new.name: Rabih az-Zubayr's Bornu state
entries_new.founder: Rabih az-Zubayr, Sudanese warlord, adventurer and slave trader
entries_new.stopped_by: French army under Lamy and Gentil at Kousséri, 1900
entries_new.pop: Army grew from 400 to 5,000
entries_new.challenge: Sultanate of Bagirmi; Kanem-Bornu; France
entries_new.mechanism: A raider built an army from plunder, then replaced an old dynasty with a military government funded by heavy taxation.
entries_new.story:
Rabih az-Zubayr, a Sudanese warlord and slave trader, took a small force west after his commander's defeat by Egyptian and British forces. Over about a decade his army grew from 400 to 5,000 through raiding. In 1892 to 1894 he conquered the Kanem-Bornu Empire and ran it as a military dictatorship. His taxation was efficient and brutal and, according to Wikipedia, cut food production.
France sent expeditions in 1899 to 1900, and a French army with local allies killed him at Kousséri in 1900. The old dynasty returned under French control. He is remembered both for his brutal rule and his resistance to European colonialism.
